# IM construction

This page shows a toy example of how to construct a possibilistic inferential model (IM) for a random effect model.

\begin{align*}
    X_{ij} &= Z_i+\epsilon_{ij}, 
    \\     
    X_{ij} &| Z_i \sim N(Z_i, \sigma^2_\epsilon), \\
    Z_i & \sim N(0, \sigma^2_Z). 
\end{align*} for $i = 1, \cdots, m$ and $j = 1, \cdots, n$.

For example, if we set $m=5, n=3$, here is one example of the data.

```{r}
m <- 5 
n <- 3
sig2 <- 7
tau2 <- 5
x <- sqrt(sig2) * matrix(rnorm(m * n), nrow=m) + sqrt(tau2) * rnorm(m)
boxplot(c(x[1,]), c(x[2,]), c(x[3,]), c(x[4,]), c(x[5,]))
```

## Relative likelihood

To construct an inferential model, we first construct the relative likelihood: $$ R(x, \theta) = \frac{p_{\theta}(x)}{\sup_{\vartheta} p_\vartheta(x)} = \exp \left( \log p_\theta(x) - \log p_{\hat{\theta}}(x) \right),$$ where $p_{\theta}(x)$ is the likelihood function. The marginal log likelihood is \begin{align*} 
\log P(X) &=
-\frac{mn}{2} \log(2 \pi) - \frac{m(n-1)}{2} \log(\sigma^2_\epsilon) \\
& - \frac{m}{2} \log(\sigma^2_\epsilon + n \sigma^2_Z) - \frac{\sum_i \sum_j (x_{ij} - \bar{x_{i\cdot}})^2}{2\sigma^2_\epsilon} - \frac{n \sum_i \bar{x_{i\cdot}^2}}{2(\sigma^2_\epsilon + n\sigma^2_Z)}.
\end{align*} The maximum likelihood estimators are: \begin{align*}
    \hat{\sigma}^2_\epsilon &= \frac{\sum_i \sum_j (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2}{m(n-1)}, \\
    \hat{\sigma}^2_Z &= \frac{1}{n} \left( \frac{n \sum_i \bar{x}_i^2}{m} - \frac{\sum_i \sum_j (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2 }{m(n-1)} \right),
\end{align*} where $\bar{x}_i = \frac{1}{n} \sum_j x_{ij}$. Now we have all the pieces to calculate the relative likelihood.

## Contour function

The next step is a validation step:

$$\pi_x(\theta) = P_\theta(R(X, \theta) \le R(x, \theta)).$$

The code below finds the contour function $\pi_x(\theta)$ given observation $x$ and the parameter of interest $\theta$.

```{r}
get.suff.stat <- function(x) {
  
  xbar.i <- rowMeans(x)
  xbar <- mean(x)
  out <- c(sum((x - xbar.i)**2), sum((xbar.i)**2))
  return(out)
  
}

# marginal loglikelihood without the latent variable
logrellik <- function(x, sig2, tau2){
  m <- nrow(x)
  n <- ncol(x)
  S <- get.suff.stat(x)
  sig2_hat <- S[1]/(m*(n-1))
  tau2_hat <- (n*S[2]/m - S[1]/(m*(n-1)))/n
  
  f <- function(u) {
    
    s2 <- exp(u[1])
    t2 <- exp(u[2])
    o1 <- m * (n - 1) * log(s2) + m * log(s2 + n * t2)
    o2 <- S[1] / s2 + n * S[2] / (s2 + n * t2)
    return( -(o1 + o2) / 2 )
    
  }
  
  out <- list( logrellik = f(c(sig2, tau2)) - f(c(sig2_hat, tau2_hat)))
  return(out)
} 



```

## Example demonstration

Now assume we observe data from $m=50$ groups and each grup has $n=5$ repeated measures. Let's plot the contour function.

```{r}
m <- 30
n <- 5
sig2 <- .5 
tau2 <- .6
size <- 100

thetaZ <- thetaE <- seq(.5, 1, by=.02)
pi <- outer(thetaZ, thetaE)

e <- sqrt(sig2) * matrix(rnorm(m * n), nrow=m) 
z <- sqrt(tau2) * rnorm(m)
x <- e+z

for (i in seq_along(thetaZ)){
  for (j in seq_along(thetaE)){
    
    ttau2 <- thetaZ[i]^2
    ssig2 <- thetaE[j]^2
    
    LHS <- rep(NA, size)
    
    for (s in 1:size){
      
      Z <- sqrt(ttau2) * rnorm(m)
      E <- sqrt(ssig2) * matrix(rnorm(m * n), nrow = m)
      X <- E + Z
      
      LHS[s] <- logrellik(X, ssig2, ttau2)$logrellik
      
    }
    RHS <- logrellik(x, ssig2, ttau2)$logrellik
    pi[i, j] <- mean(LHS <= RHS)
    
  }
}

plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(.5, 1), ylim = c(.5, 1), xlab = expression(sigma[Z]), ylab = expression(sigma[E]), main=paste0("m=",m,", n=",n))
contour(thetaZ, thetaE, pi, drawlabels=TRUE, add=TRUE)
contour(thetaZ, thetaE, pi, levels=c(.1,1),add=TRUE, col="magenta")
points(sqrt(tau2), sqrt(sig2), col="red", pch=19)

```

As shown above, the contour plot is now two-dimensional. The red dot is where the true variances are, and the two magenta curves mark the $90\%$ confidence region.



# Reference

Martin, Ryan. (2026). Possibilistic inferential models: a review. *Journal of American Statistical Association,* 121 (553): 807-826. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09007).
